questions.q: A repository finds out that book 42 does not exist. What should it throw?
questions.explain: Code deep inside the app should not need to know HTTP. It says what went wrong with a typed error. One function in the HTTP layer, toErrorResponse, maps each type to its status code.
options: new HttpError(404, "not_found", "Book 42 not found")
new NotFoundError("Book 42"), and let the HTTP layer choose the status code
Nothing: it should return { status: 404 }
new Error("404")

questions.q: Which mapping does the BookStore's toErrorResponse use?
questions.explain: 400: fix your request, the issues say what is wrong. 404: the thing in the URL does not exist. 409: the request is fine but clashes with the current data. Unknown errors are still a generic 500.
options: ValidationError 422, NotFoundError 404, ConflictError 400
ValidationError 400, NotFoundError 404, ConflictError 409
ValidationError 400, NotFoundError 410, ConflictError 500
All three become 500

questions.q: Which situation is a 409 Conflict in the BookStore?
questions.explain: The order is well-formed, but it clashes with the current data. The same goes for creating a second author with a name that already exists. A wrong field is 400, and a missing resource in the URL is 404.
options: The body has "quantity": "two"
The URL asks for book 999, which does not exist
A client orders 5 copies, but only 1 is left in stock
The server has a bug in a repository

questions.q: Why do the helpers text and whole push a message to issues and return a placeholder, instead of throwing?
questions.explain: After all fields are read, done throws one ValidationError with every issue. The client can fix everything in one go. The placeholders are never saved, because done throws first.
options: Because throwing is slow
So one request gets all its problems reported at once, not one per attempt
Because type guards are not allowed to throw
So invalid values can still be saved with the placeholder

questions.q: Why does every check have a maximum, such as a title of at most 200 characters and a quantity of at most 100?
questions.explain: Valid-looking but huge values waste memory and storage, or place absurd orders. A check that only looks at the type is not enough: always set a sensible range.
options: Because PostgreSQL text columns cannot hold more
Because a 5 MB "title" or a quantity of a billion is wrong too, and can hurt the server or the business
Because JSON strings are limited to 200 characters
To make the error messages shorter

questions.q: A client sends {"name": "Ada", "id": 1, "isAdmin": true} to POST /authors. What does parseNewAuthor return?
questions.explain: The parser builds a new object from the fields it checked. Extra fields like id or isAdmin are dropped here and can never reach the database.
options: The whole body, because name is valid
{ name: "Ada" }: a new object with only the checked fields
A ValidationError for the unknown fields
{ name: "Ada", id: 1 }, because id is a real column

questions.explain: It is the real database engine with no server to install. It keeps data in memory, or in a folder if you give it one. The SQL is the same, so moving to a PostgreSQL server later changes one file.
options: A lightweight SQL dialect that looks like PostgreSQL
Real PostgreSQL compiled to WebAssembly, running inside your Node.js process
An in-memory Map with an SQL-like API
A client that connects to a PostgreSQL server over the network

questions.q: Why is PGlite installed with npm install @electric-sql/pglite, without -D?
questions.explain: TypeScript, tsx and @types/node are development tools (-D). The database library is used by the server when it runs, so it goes in dependencies.
options: Because -D does not work with scoped packages
Because the running app needs it, while -D is for tools only needed during development
Because it is a global command
It does not matter; both put it in devDependencies

questions.q: author_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES authors (id). What does REFERENCES do?
questions.explain: A foreign key makes the database protect its own data. Even a bug in your TypeScript cannot create a book pointing at a missing author, or delete an author who still has books.
options: It copies the author's name into the books table
It is a foreign key: PostgreSQL refuses a book whose author does not exist
It makes author_id unique
It deletes the books when the author is deleted

questions.q: The code already validates bodies. Why also add UNIQUE, CHECK (stock >= 0) and foreign keys to the tables?
questions.explain: Validation checks the shape of one request. Only the database sees all the data at once, so rules like "no duplicate names" and "stock never below 0" belong there too. Both layers work together.
options: They are required by PGlite
The database then protects its data even when the application code has a bug, or two requests race
They make queries faster
They replace the need to validate bodies

questions.q: Why do the migrations use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS?
questions.explain: openDatabase runs the migrations every time the server starts. Without IF NOT EXISTS, the second start would fail because the tables are already there. Real projects use a migration tool that remembers which steps ran.
options: So the table is dropped and recreated with fresh data
So they are safe to run on every start: an existing table is left alone
Because PostgreSQL requires it
So the table exists only in memory

questions.q: PostgreSQL throws an error with code: "23505" when creating an author. What happened, and what does the repository throw?
questions.explain: 23505 means "unique rule broken" and becomes a 409 conflict. 23503 means "foreign key broken", which the book repository reports as a 400 validation issue (authorId 7 does not exist).
options: A foreign key was broken; it throws ValidationError
A unique rule was broken (the name exists); it throws ConflictError
The table is missing; it throws NotFoundError
The connection failed; it throws HttpError(500)

questions.q: search comes from a query string. Which query is safe?
questions.explain: With $1, the SQL and the value travel to PostgreSQL separately, so the value is only ever data, never SQL. Pasting it into the string, even with quotes removed or changed, lets crafted input rewrite the query: SQL injection.
options: db.query(`SELECT title FROM books WHERE title = '${search}'`)
db.query("SELECT title FROM books WHERE title = '" + search.replace("'", "") + "'")
db.query("SELECT title FROM books WHERE title = $1", [search])
db.query(`SELECT title FROM books WHERE title = "${search}"`)

questions.q: The book repository writes `SELECT ${COLUMNS} FROM books WHERE id = $1`. Why is pasting COLUMNS into the SQL safe?
questions.explain: The danger is outside input in SQL. A constant you wrote yourself cannot be changed by a client. Every value from outside still goes in as $1, $2, …
options: Because template strings escape values automatically
Because COLUMNS is a fixed string written in the code, never user input
Because column names cannot contain quotes
It is not safe; it should be $2

questions.q: Why does placing an order take the stock and insert the order in one SQL statement?
questions.explain: With a separate "read stock" and "write order", both requests could read "1 left" and both succeed. UPDATE … WHERE stock >= $2 inside the same statement only changes the book if there is enough stock.
options: Because PGlite allows only one query per request
Two customers may buy the last copy at the same moment; one statement runs as a single step, so stock cannot be sold twice
Because it is shorter to write
To avoid using $1 parameters

questions.q: Where does an order's total_cents come from?
questions.explain: The price comes from the database, never from the client, so nobody can send their own price. The client only says which book and how many.
options: From totalCents in the request body
From priceCents in the request body, times the quantity
From the book's price_cents in the database, times the quantity
From the client's previous order

questions.q: Why is moving from PGlite to a PostgreSQL server (with pg) only one new file?
questions.explain: Repositories get a Queryable through their constructor: "run this SQL with these parameters and give me rows". connectPostgres wraps a pg.Pool in that shape, and no repository changes.
options: Because pg and PGlite are the same package
Because every repository depends only on the small Queryable interface, and both can be wrapped to fit it
Because the repositories read DATABASE_URL themselves
Because TypeScript converts PGlite calls to pg calls

questions.q: DATABASE_URL looks like postgres://postgres:PASSWORD@localhost:5440/bookstore. How should you handle it?
questions.explain: The URL contains the password. It belongs in the environment of the server. The lesson even creates a random password in a shell variable, so it never appears in a file.
options: Put it in config.ts as the default value
Commit it in a .env file so the team has it
Set it only in the server's environment; never commit it, log it or put it in an error message
Send it to the client in the 500 response, to help debugging
